name: Daria Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can give me the public version and the private one. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach guitar and ukulele at the Riverside Music Academy, mostly beginners, kids from about seven up and a few adults who always wanted to learn. I do back-to-back half-hour lessons from three till eight, tuning nine guitars a day and saying 'thumb behind the neck' about a hundred times. On Friday nights I play acoustic covers with my friend Hana at two restaurants in the old town. I'm honestly still learning myself; the advanced students go to Paul, not me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pretty good. The academy charges parents a lot, so it pays its teachers well, and the restaurant gigs are cash plus dinner. Kofi (my boyfriend) is an electrician, and we're saving for a house deposit; my share alone would cover about eight months. I use AI now and then, mostly to write the termly reports to parents, which I used to hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's handy for paperwork and that's about it. Kids still need someone to move their fingers onto the right fret, and I'd say that to any parent who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, because our house plan stays on track. The things that would still bother me are normal: the academy raising prices and losing pupils, or me never getting good enough to teach the advanced kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching my five afternoons and the Friday gigs. I'd use the report tool every term and save the hours for practice. Kofi and I would keep putting money aside and probably buy a small house in the next two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Settled, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the academy might lose pupils. Is that happening already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Two families left last term because money's tight, and Mr Brennan (the academy owner) was grumpy about it for a week. If it got worse, the new teachers like me would lose hours first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time the report tool saves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practise, honestly. I want to take over some of Paul's intermediate students next year, and I'm not quick enough on scales yet. That's two hours a week back.

The academy **losing pupils** would cost new teachers like me hours first.
do: Keep teaching **five afternoons** and Friday restaurant gigs.
Use the **report tool** each term and spend saved hours practising.
Buy a **small house** with Kofi within two years.
feel: **Settled**, mostly, because her plans stay on track.

steps.text: Keep teaching five afternoons at Riverside and Friday restaurant gigs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teaching is changing and good teachers will change with it. I'd probably share a sensible article on it and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, beginner lessons are exactly what an app can do now. A phone listens to a kid strumming, tells them the chord's wrong and gives them a game for practice, for a tenth of what my music school charges. I teach beginners, so I'm the one whose hours shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Brennan this term which way he's thinking. Once a few teachers I trust start using the tutor apps, I'd use them too, so my lessons are the human bit on top of the app. I'd also take a few more Friday and Saturday gigs with Hana, because playing in a room isn't something the app can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. Not panicky, because Kofi's job is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house plan in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still buy, but something smaller, maybe a flat instead of a house. I wouldn't want a mortgage that only works if I keep all my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the academy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta (the academy's piano teacher for little ones) is 58 and she's even more beginner-focused than I am. She hates computers. I'd worry she'd be the first one Mr Brennan lets go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government quickly, like help for people retraining. I wouldn't panic in public, but I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my teaching job is finished by 2028. Parents will get an AI teacher for almost nothing. The gigs with Hana last until robots in 2031, but that's cash on Fridays, not a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Kofi about me training as an electrician alongside him, because wiring houses needs hands for longer than teaching does. I'd keep teaching until the end and save every spare bit. We'd put the house on hold, which kills me, but I wouldn't take a mortgage into that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach dropped just hearing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the gigs and Kofi's work buy us time, not safety. Kofi's job lasts a bit longer than mine because it's hands-on. If I trained with him, we'd both have those extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said good teachers would change. Does that hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, and I know it. In the slow one I could adapt. With AGI in two years there's nothing to adapt to.

I wouldn't **panic in public**, but I'd say that.
think: Restaurant gigs with Hana last until **2031**, but they're cash on Fridays, not a living.
do: Look into **training as an electrician** alongside Kofi.
Keep teaching until the end and **save** every spare bit.
feel: **Alarmed**, her stomach dropping on hearing it.

fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** outright and says so plainly.

steps.text: Look into training as an electrician alongside Kofi

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. I'd tell other teachers to have a second skill by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get three or four years more of teaching, and I'd want a plan B by then. I'd rather it be music-related if possible, maybe running group music sessions in care homes, where people want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tutor apps as soon as the academy brings them in, to stay useful. I'd start a short course in music for care homes, which a woman at church runs. And we'd buy the flat, but only with a small mortgage Kofi could carry alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's manageable. I'd have time to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care homes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My gran was in one and the happiest hour of her week was a woman playing old songs on a guitar. Nobody's going to want a robot singing to their gran, at least not for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, probably. Kofi and I go away twice a year, and we'd make it once. That money would go into the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for teachers to move into new roles, and that we should start the conversation now. I'd say that at a staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief. I'd have time to get better, teach intermediate students and build the care home work. By 2036 I'd be 37, maybe with kids of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and use the apps when they're proven. I'd do the care home course in a couple of years. Kofi and I would buy a small house as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still the same end point, but there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Kofi's work is hands-on, so it lasts longer, and with ten years we'd have a paid-down house. I'd still want them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently because of the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at guitar, which I'm not yet. If I'm going to play for people in care homes or at weddings, I want to be someone people ask for by name.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my teaching would just end and the house plan would end with it. What would help is paid retraining, the kind where you can still pay rent while you learn a trade, like electrical work with Kofi.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. Some of my seven-year-olds are learning more from me than guitar, like how to keep going when something's hard. I don't know if an app teaches that.
